patient.name: Hamid Rahimi
patient.complaint: Admitted confused, with 2 months of cough and weight loss; says 'Don't tell my family, and no tablets'
background: Mild Alzheimer's dementia, manages at home with help
Lives in Ealing with his daughter Parisa and two grandchildren aged 4 and 7
No lasting power of attorney and no advance decision

diagnosis.exam: Here 'diagnosis' means recognising the ethical issue. Expect 'Which ethical principle is most relevant?' or 'Which element of capacity is lacking?', with long statement-style options.

points: Hamid, 74, brought in by his daughter: confused for 3 days.
Two months of cough, night sweats, 6 kg weight loss.
He keeps pulling out his cannula.

visual.title: Hamid's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right upper zone cavity: pulmonary TB until proven otherwise. TB is a notifiable disease.

points: Sputum smear: **acid-fast bacilli seen**. Pulmonary TB.
Hamid: '**Don't tell my family.** And I don't want tablets.'
He lives with two young grandchildren.

steps.q: Hamid refuses treatment. Which principle are you weighing against his wish to refuse?
steps.r: Respecting his refusal is **autonomy**; treating him for his own good is **beneficence**. These are the two pillars in tension here.

steps.title: The four pillars in Hamid's case
head: Pillar
Meaning
In Hamid's case
rows: His refusal of tablets; his wish for secrecy
Avoid needless restraint; avoid infecting others
Public health: protect contacts and the wider community

steps.text: Every ethics SBA starts by asking: **does this patient have capacity for this decision?** If yes, autonomy wins, even if the choice is unwise.

steps.title: Recognising the ethical question
nodes: Is there a decision to be made?
Does the patient have capacity for it?
Yes → respect their autonomous choice
No → decide in their best interests (MCA)
Information sharing? → check confidentiality exceptions

steps.text: Dementia, delirium or a learning disability do **not** mean someone lacks capacity. Capacity is **decision-specific** and must be assessed, never assumed from a diagnosis.

investigation.exam: Here 'investigation' means assessing capacity. Expect 'Which is the most appropriate next step?' (assess capacity for this decision) or 'Which part of the test does he fail?'.

steps.title: Hamid's bloods
steps.text: Hyponatraemia and infection are driving a delirium on top of his dementia: a reversible cause of lost capacity.

points: The registrar assesses capacity for one decision: **starting TB treatment**.
She explains simply, in Dari with an interpreter.
Uses the **four-stage test**.

steps.title: Four-stage capacity test
nodes: Understand the relevant information?
Retain it long enough to decide?
Weigh it up to make a decision?
Communicate the decision?
Fails any one → lacks capacity for this decision

points: Hamid repeats that TB is 'a chest infection'.
Five minutes later he has **forgotten** the conversation.
He cannot say what happens without treatment.

visual.title: Capacity test elements met (day 1)
visual.label: Hamid 1 of 4
visual.caption: He can communicate but cannot understand, retain or weigh. All four are needed, so he lacks capacity for this decision now.

steps.q: Hamid cannot retain the information. What follows?
o: He has capacity because he can communicate
He lacks capacity for this decision at this time
He lacks capacity for all decisions
His daughter must decide for him
steps.r: Capacity is **decision- and time-specific**. Failing one element means he lacks capacity for this decision now; it may return as his delirium settles.

visual.title: Sodium and capacity over the admission
visual.caption: As the delirium clears, Hamid regains capacity, so reassess: capacity is time-specific.

steps.text: Do not ask 'does he have capacity?' in general. Ask 'does he have capacity **to make this decision, now**?' and reassess when a reversible cause improves.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate action?' with options like treating in best interests after consulting family, notifying public health, or breaching confidentiality only with a justified reason.

points: Day 1: Hamid lacks capacity; untreated TB could kill him.
No lasting power of attorney; no advance decision.
Parisa says: 'He always trusted doctors and wanted to see the children grow up.'

steps.q: Hamid lacks capacity to decide on TB treatment. What should the team do?
o: Ask Parisa to sign consent for him
Start treatment in his best interests after consulting Parisa
Wait until he regains capacity, however long
Withhold treatment because he refused it
steps.r: Under the **Mental Capacity Act**, the clinician decides in his **best interests**, using his past wishes and views of family. Relatives cannot consent for adults.

steps.title: Best interests decision
nodes: Confirm he lacks capacity for this decision
Can it wait until he regains capacity?
Find his past wishes, values and beliefs
Consult family and carers who know him
Choose the least restrictive option in his best interests

points: TB is a **notifiable disease**: the team notifies public health (UKHSA).
His grandchildren live with him and are at risk.
Public health arranges contact screening.

steps.title: Can I share this information?
nodes: Default: keep it confidential
Legal requirement (notifiable disease, court order)?
Risk of serious harm to the patient or others?
Safeguarding concern?
If yes: share only what is needed, with the right people

steps.text: Notifying TB is a **legal duty**; consent is not needed. Share the **minimum** necessary, with public health, not with neighbours or his employer.

points: Day 8: sodium normal; Hamid now passes all four elements.
He agrees to continue treatment.
Asked again, he lets the team tell Parisa the diagnosis.

steps.text: Next of kin have **no legal power** to consent for an adult who lacks capacity, unless they hold a **lasting power of attorney** for health decisions.

science.exam: Expect applied principle questions: which pillar a decision reflects, which pillars conflict, when confidentiality can be breached, and which law governs decisions for adults lacking capacity.

steps.lead: Hamid's case shows the pillars **colliding**: his autonomy against beneficence, and his secrecy against justice to his grandchildren and the public.
On day 1 Hamid failed **understand, retain and weigh**; on day 8 he passed all four. Same man, same decision, different time.
While Hamid lacked capacity, the team used his **past wishes** and Parisa's views to act in his **best interests** under the **Mental Capacity Act**.
Hamid's TB was notified because of a **legal requirement**; his grandchildren were screened because of **risk of serious harm** to others.

steps.q: A capacitous patient refuses a life-saving treatment. Which pillar must the doctor respect?
steps.r: With capacity, **autonomy** wins even over a beneficent recommendation. An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.

mcq.q: Respecting a patient's right to make their own decisions is which pillar?
Fair allocation of resources and equal treatment is which pillar?
Which is NOT part of the four-stage capacity test?
mcq.r: Understand, retain, weigh up, communicate. An unwise decision does not mean incapacity.

o: Per decision and at a point in time

mcq.q: How are decisions made for adults who lack capacity?
mcq.r: Best interests, considering past wishes and input from those who know them.

mcq.q: Which is a valid reason to breach confidentiality?
o: To help a research project without consent
mcq.r: Legal requirements such as notifiable diseases or a court order.

mcq.q: Which of these justifies disclosure without consent?
o: Curiosity of a colleague not involved
Risk of serious harm to others
mcq.r: Serious harm, safeguarding or legal requirement.

mcq.q: Which UK law governs best interests decisions for adults lacking capacity?

prompts.q: Name and define the four pillars of medical ethics.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the pillar a decision serves, and spot when two conflict.

points.p: Autonomy: respecting the patient's right to decide
points.why: With capacity, autonomy usually wins.

points.p: Beneficence: acting in the patient's best interests
points.why: Doing good for the patient.

points.p: Non-maleficence: avoiding harm
points.why: Includes not offering futile or harmful treatment.

points.p: Justice: fair allocation of resources and equal treatment
points.why: Think NICE, waiting lists, ICU beds.

points.p: They often conflict; ethics is balancing them sensibly
points.why: Classic clash: autonomy vs beneficence in a refusal.

prompts.q: A patient with capacity refuses treatment you think they need. Which pillars conflict, and which wins?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: an unwise decision is still their decision.

points.p: Autonomy versus beneficence
points.why: Respecting choice versus doing good.

points.p: With capacity, autonomy wins: respect the refusal
points.why: Even if the decision seems unwise.

prompts.q: When can patient confidentiality be breached?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three exceptions, otherwise it stays confidential.

points.p: Not absolute, but a core duty
points.why: Outside the exceptions, information stays confidential.

points.p: Risk of serious harm to the patient or others
points.why: E.g. a driver with uncontrolled epilepsy who keeps driving.

points.p: Safeguarding concerns
points.why: Children and vulnerable adults.

points.p: Legal requirement: notifiable diseases or a court order
points.why: TB, meningitis, measles must be notified.

prompts.q: Does a diagnosis of dementia mean a patient lacks capacity?

points.p: No: capacity is decision-specific
points.why: They may lack capacity for complex decisions but retain it for simple ones.

points.p: Capacity is time-specific and can fluctuate
points.why: Delirium may resolve; reassess.

points.p: It must be assessed, not assumed from a diagnosis
points.why: Learning disability and mental illness also do not equal incapacity.

prompts.q: What is the four-stage test for capacity?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fail any one and they lack capacity for that decision.

points.p: Understand the relevant information
points.why: Information must be given in a way they can follow.

points.p: Retain it
points.why: Only long enough to make the decision.

points.p: Weigh it up to make a decision
points.why: Often failed in severe anorexia or psychosis.

points.p: Communicate the decision
points.why: By any means: speech, writing, blinking.

points.p: All four must be satisfied
points.why: One failure is enough to lack capacity.

prompts.q: What makes capacity decision-specific and time-specific in practice?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the same person, a different decision or a different day.

points.p: Can lack capacity for one decision but retain it for another
points.why: Choosing lunch versus consenting to surgery.

points.p: Reassess when a reversible cause (e.g. delirium) improves
points.why: If the decision can wait, wait for capacity to return.

prompts.q: How are decisions made for an adult who lacks capacity?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the clinician decides in best interests; relatives advise.

points.p: In the patient's best interests
points.why: Not what the family would choose for themselves.

points.p: Consider previously expressed wishes, values and beliefs
points.why: A valid advance decision to refuse must be followed.

points.p: Get input from family and carers who know the patient
points.why: Relatives cannot consent unless they hold a health LPA.

points.p: Governed by the Mental Capacity Act
points.why: Not the Mental Health Act, which covers mental disorder.

prompts.q: A patient with TB asks you not to tell anyone. What do you do?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: legal duty, minimum information, right recipient.

points.p: Notify public health: TB is a notifiable disease (legal requirement)
points.why: No consent needed for statutory notification.

points.p: Share only what is needed with those who need it
points.why: Employers and neighbours are not told.

points.p: Explain to the patient what will be shared and why
points.why: Honesty preserves trust.

prompts.q: Which pillar does each scenario reflect: refusal respected, harmful drug stopped, ICU bed allocation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the pillar from the action.

points.p: Respecting a capacitous refusal: autonomy
points.why: Self-determination.

points.p: Stopping a drug causing side effects: non-maleficence
points.why: Avoiding harm.

points.p: Allocating a scarce bed fairly: justice
points.why: Fair distribution of resources.

glossary.Autonomy: The patient's right to make their own decisions about their care.
glossary.Beneficence: Acting in the patient's best interests; doing good.
glossary.Justice: Fair allocation of resources and equal treatment of patients.
glossary.Confidentiality: The duty to keep patient information private unless a recognised exception applies.
glossary.Capacity: The ability to make a specific decision at a specific time, judged by the four-stage test.
glossary.Four-stage test: Can the patient understand, retain, weigh up the information and communicate a decision?
glossary.Decision-specific: Capacity applies to one decision; a person may decide some things but not others.
glossary.Time-specific: Capacity is judged at the time of the decision and can change, for example as delirium clears.
glossary.Best interests: The basis for decisions for adults lacking capacity, using their wishes, values and the views of those close to them.
glossary.Mental Capacity Act: The 2005 law for England and Wales on assessing capacity and acting in best interests.
glossary.MCA: Mental Capacity Act 2005, the framework for adults who lack capacity.
glossary.Mental Health Act: Law allowing detention and treatment of mental disorder; separate from the Mental Capacity Act.
glossary.Lasting power of attorney: A legal document letting a chosen person make health or financial decisions if the patient loses capacity.
glossary.LPA: Lasting power of attorney, which can give a named person authority over health decisions.
glossary.Advance decision: A legally binding refusal of specific treatment, made while the person had capacity.
glossary.Next of kin: The patient's closest relative; has no legal power to consent for an adult.
glossary.Notifiable disease: An infection doctors must legally report to public health, such as TB, measles or meningitis.
glossary.UKHSA: UK Health Security Agency, the public health body that receives notifications and runs contact tracing.
glossary.Safeguarding: Protecting children and vulnerable adults from abuse or neglect; a reason to share information.
glossary.Court order: An instruction from a court, which can legally require disclosure of patient information.
glossary.Public interest: Disclosure to protect others from serious harm, which can outweigh confidentiality.
glossary.DVLA: Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency; doctors may inform it if a patient unsafe to drive keeps driving.
glossary.Delirium: An acute, fluctuating confusion from an illness, drug or metabolic cause; often reversible.
glossary.Dementia: Progressive decline in memory and thinking; does not by itself mean a person lacks capacity.
glossary.Unwise decision: A choice others disagree with; under the MCA it is not evidence of lacking capacity.
glossary.Valid consent: Consent given voluntarily by an informed person with capacity.
glossary.IMCA: Independent mental capacity advocate, appointed for serious decisions when a person lacking capacity has no one to consult.
glossary.Least restrictive option: Under the MCA, the choice that limits the person's rights and freedom the least.
glossary.GMC: General Medical Council, which sets UK doctors' professional standards on consent and confidentiality.
glossary.AFB: Acid-fast bacilli, seen on sputum staining in tuberculosis.
glossary.Contact tracing: Finding and testing people exposed to an infectious patient.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman who is a Jehovah's Witness is admitted with a bleeding duodenal ulcer. She understands that without a blood transfusion she may die. She clearly explains her reasons and repeats them consistently, and says she does not want blood under any circumstances. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg.
technique.q: Which ethical principle is most relevant to respecting her refusal?

steps.x: The principle behind respecting a refusal.

clues: She understands that without a blood transfusion she may die
steps.x: She understands, retains, weighs and communicates: she has capacity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Respecting a capacitous refusal is **autonomy**.

elim: Beneficence would push for transfusion; it is the principle being overridden.
Justice concerns fairness and resources, not her refusal.
Non-maleficence is avoiding harm; respecting refusal here risks harm.
Utility is not one of the four pillars.

steps.x: **A. Autonomy.** Capacity present means her decision stands, even if it may be fatal.

technique.stem: An 82 year old man with vascular dementia needs surgery for a fractured neck of femur. The surgeon explains the operation. He can describe the risks and benefits back accurately and says he wants the operation. Ten minutes later he cannot recall having had the conversation at all. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 142/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which element of the capacity assessment is he unable to meet?

steps.x: Which of the four stages is failed?

clues: describe the risks and benefits back accurately
cannot recall having had the conversation
steps.x: He understands and communicates, but forgets.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Retain.** He must hold it long enough to decide; here he cannot.

elim: He communicates his choice clearly.
Wisdom is not part of the test.
He repeats the risks and benefits accurately.
He weighs them in the moment; the failure is memory.

steps.x: **C. Retain.** Fail one of four and he lacks capacity for this decision.

technique.stem: A 68 year old woman is unconscious on the ward after a large stroke and needs a nasogastric tube for feeding. She has no advance decision and no lasting power of attorney. Her husband says she valued independence but always wanted every treatment that might help her recover. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her husband to give consent on her behalf
Decide in her best interests, taking account of her husband's account of her wishes
Seek a court order before any treatment
Wait until she regains capacity before feeding
Withhold feeding because she valued independence

steps.x: What to do for an adult who lacks capacity.

clues: no advance decision and no lasting power of attorney
always wanted every treatment that might help
steps.x: Lacks capacity; nobody with legal authority; family can tell us her wishes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Decide in her **best interests** under the MCA, informed by her husband's account.

elim: A spouse cannot consent for an adult without an LPA.
Court is for disputes or very serious decisions, not routine best interests care.
Feeding cannot safely wait for an uncertain recovery.
Her stated wish was to have treatment that might help.

steps.x: **B. Best interests, with family input.** Relatives inform; the clinician decides.

technique.stem: A 56 year old man with capacity has severe peripheral arterial disease and a gangrenous foot. His surgeon recommends below-knee amputation to prevent fatal sepsis. He understands the risks and refuses, saying he would rather die with both legs. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which two ethical principles are most directly in conflict?

steps.x: Which two pillars clash?
A capacitous choice against a doctor's recommendation for his good.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: His **autonomy** against the surgeon's **beneficence**.

elim: No resource allocation issue, so justice is not central.
Neither of these is the patient's own choice.
No fairness or resource question.
Confidentiality is not at issue; no information is being shared.

steps.x: **A. Autonomy and beneficence.** With capacity, autonomy wins.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman with capacity has metastatic breast cancer. Her oncologist offers further chemotherapy. She says she understands that it might extend her life by some months, but she would rather spend her remaining time at home without side effects. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 124/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which ethical principle is most important in accepting her decision?
practice.e: A capacitous patient's informed choice to decline treatment is an exercise of autonomy, which must be respected.

steps.x: The principle behind accepting her choice.

clues: would rather spend her remaining time at home
steps.x: Informed, capacitous refusal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Autonomy.**

elim: Beneficence would favour the chemotherapy.
No resource allocation question.
Avoiding side effects is her reason, but accepting her choice is about autonomy.
Veracity is truth-telling, not one of the four pillars.

steps.x: **A. Autonomy.**

practice.stem: A 70 year old man on the ward has developed acute kidney injury. His consultant stops his ibuprofen and gentamicin, saying the drugs are now doing more harm than good. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which ethical principle is the consultant mainly acting on?
practice.e: Stopping drugs because they are causing harm is non-maleficence: avoiding harm.

steps.x: Which pillar drives stopping the drugs?
The drugs are harming him.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Non-maleficence.**

elim: The patient is not making a choice here.
Beneficence is actively doing good; the action here is removing harm.
No information is being shared.
No resources are being allocated.

steps.x: **E. Non-maleficence.**

practice.stem: A hospital has one intensive care bed left and two patients referred at the same time. The intensivists decide using a published, consistent set of criteria based on likely benefit, without regard to the patients' jobs or social status.
practice.q: Which ethical principle does this approach mainly reflect?
practice.e: Fair, consistent allocation of a scarce resource with equal treatment is justice.

steps.x: Principle behind allocating a scarce bed.

clues: without regard to the patients' jobs or social status
steps.x: Scarce resource, fair process, equal treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Justice.**

elim: Neither patient is making the decision.
Beneficence is about one patient's good, not fair distribution.
Fidelity (keeping promises) is not a core pillar.
Avoiding harm is not the main point of the allocation process.

steps.x: **D. Justice.**

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman with severe anorexia nervosa refuses nasogastric feeding. She understands that her low weight could cause cardiac arrest, can repeat this back, and states her decision clearly. She says that the risk does not apply to her because she is not thin. Her pulse rate is 42 bpm and BP 82/50 mmHg.
practice.q: Which element of the capacity test is she most likely unable to meet?
o: Make a decision others agree with
practice.e: She understands, retains and communicates, but her illness stops her applying the information to herself: she cannot weigh it up.

steps.x: Which of the four stages is failed?

clues: does not apply to her because she is not thin
steps.x: Understands, retains, communicates; cannot use it for herself.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Weigh up.**

elim: She communicates clearly.
Agreement with others is not part of the test.
She repeats it back, so she retains it.
She can explain the risk, so she understands it.

steps.x: **E. Weigh up.** Classic in anorexia and psychosis.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man has newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis confirmed on sputum testing. He asks the doctor not to tell anyone, including public health, because he is worried about losing his job. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the strongest justification for disclosing his diagnosis without consent?
practice.e: TB is a notifiable disease, so there is a legal requirement to notify public health. His employer and family have no right to the information.

steps.x: The basis for breaching confidentiality.

clues: not to tell anyone, including public health
steps.x: A notifiable disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Legal requirement** (notifiable disease).

elim: He has capacity, so best interests is not the basis.
Employers have no right to his diagnosis.
Audit does not justify disclosure without consent here.
Family requests do not justify disclosure.

steps.x: **C. Legal requirement.** Notifiable diseases and court orders.

practice.stem: An 84 year old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease is admitted with a urinary tract infection. She clearly chooses which meals she wants and decides she wants her daughter to visit, but cannot understand or weigh up the options for changing where she lives. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which statement best describes her capacity?
o: She has capacity for all decisions because she can make some
She lacks capacity for all decisions because she has dementia
She lacks capacity only for the decision about where to live
Her capacity cannot be assessed while she has an infection
Her daughter's view decides her capacity
practice.e: Capacity is decision-specific: she can make simple choices but lacks capacity for the complex decision about her residence.

steps.x: How does capacity apply across her decisions?

clues: clearly chooses which meals she wants
cannot understand or weigh up the options for changing where she lives
steps.x: Capable of some decisions, not others.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Capacity is **decision-specific**.

elim: Capacity for simple decisions does not transfer to complex ones.
Dementia alone never means global incapacity.
Capacity can be assessed now; it may need reassessing later.
Capacity is assessed by the clinician, not decided by family.

steps.x: **C. Lacks capacity only for where to live.**

practice.stem: A 76 year old man is admitted with pneumonia and new confusion. He refuses intravenous antibiotics, shouting that the nurses are poisoning him. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 104/62 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Accept his refusal and document it
Ask his son to consent for him
Assess his capacity to decide about antibiotics
Detain him under the Mental Health Act
practice.e: Delirium may impair capacity, so first assess his capacity for this specific decision. Only then accept the refusal or act in his best interests.

steps.x: The next step before acting on a refusal.
Delirium from sepsis and hyponatraemia may remove capacity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Assess capacity** for this decision.

elim: You cannot accept the refusal until you know he has capacity.
Relatives cannot consent for an adult without an LPA.
The Mental Health Act treats mental disorder, not pneumonia.
Treating without assessing capacity is not lawful in a non-emergency.

steps.x: **C. Assess capacity.** Always the first step.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with a moderate learning disability needs a decision about a dental extraction under general anaesthetic. Her carer says she 'obviously cannot decide anything for herself'. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to assessing her capacity?
o: Accept the carer's view that she lacks capacity
Assume she lacks capacity because of her learning disability
Base capacity on her IQ score
Use the four-stage test for this specific decision
practice.e: Capacity must be assessed for the specific decision using the four-stage test, with information given in a way she can understand. It is never assumed from a diagnosis.

steps.x: How to assess capacity.

clues: obviously cannot decide anything for herself
steps.x: A tempting assumption from a diagnosis and a carer's view.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Use the **four-stage test** for this decision.

elim: The carer's opinion is not a capacity assessment.
A diagnosis never proves incapacity.
IQ does not define capacity.
Any clinician proposing the treatment can assess capacity.

steps.x: **E. Four-stage test for this decision.** Never assume incapacity from a diagnosis.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man is drowsy after a severe stroke and lacks capacity to decide about a gastrostomy. He made no advance decision and has no lasting power of attorney. His wife and son disagree about what he would want. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 148/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate way to make this decision?
o: Follow the wishes of his son, as the closest blood relative
Follow the wishes of his wife, as next of kin
Postpone all decisions until he regains capacity
Take a majority vote of the family
Use a best interests decision based on his past wishes and both relatives' views
practice.e: Under the Mental Capacity Act the treating clinician decides in his best interests, considering his past wishes, values and beliefs and the views of those who know him.

steps.x: Who decides for an adult lacking capacity?

clues: disagree about what he would want
steps.x: No one has legal authority; family views differ.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Best interests**, informed by his wishes and both relatives.

elim: Blood relationship gives no legal power.
Next of kin has no legal power to consent.
Nutrition decisions cannot wait indefinitely.
Families advise; they do not vote.

steps.x: **E. Best interests decision.** If disagreement persists, seek mediation or the court.

practice.stem: A 48 year old bus driver has had two unprovoked seizures. His neurologist has told him he must not drive and must inform the DVLA. Two weeks later his wife tells the GP he is still driving his bus route. The GP's attempts to persuade him fail. He has capacity. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate action for the GP?
o: Do nothing, as disclosure needs his consent
Inform his employer directly without telling him
Inform the DVLA, telling him first that this will happen
Wait until he has another seizure
practice.e: Continuing to drive puts others at risk of serious harm, which justifies disclosure. The GP should tell the patient before informing the DVLA.

steps.x: Can the GP breach confidentiality, and how?
Risk of serious harm to the public; persuasion has failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Breach on grounds of **serious harm to others**: inform the DVLA, telling him first.

elim: Confidentiality is not absolute when others face serious harm.
The DVLA, not the employer, is the right body, and he should be told.
The police are not the appropriate first recipient.
Waiting risks a crash and harm to passengers.

steps.x: **C. Inform the DVLA, telling him first.**

practice.stem: A 6 year old boy is seen in the emergency department with a spiral fracture of the humerus. His mother says he fell off the sofa. There are bruises of different ages on his back. She asks the doctor not to tell anyone. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate action?
o: Discharge with fracture clinic follow-up only
Keep the information confidential as requested
Tell the school about the injury
Wait for a second injury before acting
practice.e: Bruises of different ages and an injury that does not fit the story raise a safeguarding concern, a recognised reason to share information without consent.

steps.x: Confidentiality versus a child at risk.
Mechanism does not fit; normal clotting; possible non-accidental injury.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Safeguarding** referral.

elim: Discharging ignores a possible abused child.
Safeguarding overrides the request for confidentiality.
The school is not the right body to receive this.
Waiting risks serious harm.

steps.x: **B. Safeguarding team.**

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman is unconscious after a cardiac arrest and needs ongoing treatment on intensive care. She has no advance decision and no lasting power of attorney. Her doctors consult her partner about her values before deciding on treatment in her best interests. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which legal framework governs this decision?
practice.e: Best interests decisions for adults lacking capacity are governed in the UK by the Mental Capacity Act. The Mental Health Act covers detention and treatment for mental disorder.
